title: Building Rainforest Rampage for Brutal Derby – my AI-assisted workflow
author: Dense-Bar-2341
selftext:
I've been working on **Rainforest Rampage**, one of the new arenas in my indie car-combat game, Brutal Derby.

For this map I wanted a dense forest/logging environment with muddy roads, cabins, rocks, fallen trees, logging structures and lots of environmental details — something completely different from my desert, snow and industrial arenas.

I'm developing the game solo, so AI has become a pretty important part of my workflow.

🤖 **Some of the tools I'm using:**

• **Tripo AI** – generating base 3D models and environment assets, which I then optimize, modify and integrate into the game.

• **Suno** – creating original music and experimenting with different soundtrack styles for the game.

• **AI coding assistants** – helping with Unity/C# development, prototyping systems, tools, shaders and speeding up repetitive programming work.

• **AI image generation** – concept art, references, textures, UI ideas and references for 3D asset generation.

The final level design, terrain, lighting, vegetation, asset placement, gameplay, optimization and integration are all done in **Unity 6.5**.

AI doesn't build the game for me — but it lets me work more like a small team while still being a solo developer.

Rainforest Rampage is still WIP, but it's already becoming one of my favorite arenas in the game.

I'd be interested to hear how other solo developers are using AI in their production pipelines.

comments.author: Haman24
comments.body:
I'm in a similar solo dev boat, and your setup is smart. That split between AI for the raw material and your own polish for the final touch is exactly how to use it effectively. It’s basically like having an extra team member just for asset generation. I’ve been using Rapid Assets recently, and it’s become a staple in my concept-to-export pipeline. The ability to generate and tweak 3D props and environments from a prompt, then get them ready for Unity or Blender without jumping between a million tools just saves so much of that initial blocking-in time. Feels less like outsourcing and more like an extension of the workspace.

For your dense forest environment, are you finding it’s the concepting stage or the actual asset creation that’s eating up the most time?
